div.head: Ps Cn for 27.2
div.ab: Uulpes et lupi nec foreste nec ueneris habentur, et proinde eorum interfectio nulli emendationi subiacet; si tamen infra limites occiduntur, fractio sit regalis chacee et mitius emendetur.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 625 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)
div.ab: Foxes and wolves are held to be neither of the forest nor of venison, and therefore their killing is subject to no compensation; if however they are killed within the bounds, let it be a breach of the royal chase, and let it be compensated more mildly.

note.seg: vgl. lupos et uulpes et alias huiusmodi nociuas bestias; Cartul. de Novo Monast. 79. Doch verlieh Richard I. Fuchsjagd im Forst als Privileg; Fisher Forest of Essex 8. Den Wolf vertilgt die Krone seit dem 10. Jh., um 1178 luporum comprehensores besoldend (Dial. scacc. II 6; vgl. Hughes p. 216); vgl. Freeman Norm. conq. IV 608; Strutt ed. Hone Sports p. 19; Hn 90, 2; Cal. of Patent rolls 1272—81 p. 435; Turner p. xiii

cf. lupos et uulpes et alias huiusmodi nociuas bestias; Cartul. de Novo Monast. 79. But Richard I granted fox-hunting in the forest as a privilege; Fisher, Forest of Essex 8. The Crown exterminates the wolf from the 10th century on, paying luporum comprehensores around 1178 (Dial. scacc. II 6; cf. Hughes p. 216); cf. Freeman, Norm. conq. IV 608; Strutt ed. Hone, Sports p. 19; Hn 90, 2; Cal. of Patent rolls 1272–81 p. 435; Turner p. xiii
Vgl. Gl Wolf 1. 2a; über königliches Amt der Wolfsvertilgung s. Round King’s serjeants 293ff.
Cf. Gl Wolf 1. 2a; on the royal office of wolf-destroying see Round King’s serjeants 293ff.
